subject: AI & Agents
title: The Objectivity Illusion
description: A short lesson to help you apply The Objectivity Illusion.

hook.text: People trust AI decisions because machines seem objective. But objectivity is an illusion.

buildup.text: Every AI system reflects choices: what data to use, what to optimize, whose values to encode.

discovery.text: A recidivism prediction tool rated Black defendants as higher risk. The data reflected systemic inequity.

twist.text: Calling AI 'objective' launders human biases through a machine, making them harder to challenge.

climax.text: The most dangerous myth is that algorithms are neutral. They encode the priorities of their creators.

punchline.text: There's no view from nowhere. Not even for machines.

quiz.question: Why is the idea that AI is 'objective' dangerous?
options: It disguises human biases as neutral machine decisions
Objectivity is never a concern in AI

details.summary: People often assume AI decisions are objective because they come from machines. In reality, every AI system reflects the subjective choices made during data collection, feature selection, and model design.
details.whyItMatters: The objectivity illusion lets biased systems escape accountability. Recognizing AI as inherently subjective empowers people to demand transparency and challenge unfair outcomes.
takeaways: AI decisions appear objective but reflect human design choices
Data selection and feature engineering embed subjective values
The illusion of objectivity shields AI from proper scrutiny

faq.question: Why do people believe AI is more objective than humans?
faq.answer: Machines seem impartial because they lack emotions. But every AI system embodies human choices about what data to use, which features matter, and what outcomes to optimize, all of which are subjective.

faq.question: How can we challenge the myth of AI objectivity?
faq.answer: Demand transparency about training data, design choices, and performance disparities. Require impact assessments and independent audits, just as we do for other consequential decision-making systems.
